sections.h:
This research on the theme of prayer among the «poor of God» in the Bible does not claim to be an exhaustive analysis, but aims to be an attempt at synthesizing the essential data that the biblical tradition offers on this theme.

The book comprises ten chapters. The first studies the poor of God of the Old Testament; the second analyzes the characteristics proper to their prayer; the third highlights the obstacles that hinder prayer; the fourth and fifth chapters address the figure of Jesus as «poor of God» and his personal prayer; the sixth examines the prayers of Jesus; the seventh and eighth are dedicated to Mary as the ideal «poor woman» of the Kingdom and to her prayer, the Magnificat; the ninth chapter outlines the identity of the Christian as «poor of God»; the tenth, finally, analyzes the proper prayer of the Christian: the Our Father.

Introduction

Who are the «poor of God» in the Old Testament? The first type of poverty spoken of in the Bible is socioeconomic poverty, a difficult reality that can have various causes: war, famine, unjust economic practices.

In subsequent biblical literature, however, the concept of «poor» takes on a profound spiritual and religious content. In this spiritualized use, «poor» designates one who recognizes himself as a creature of God, dependent on Him, who does not rely on his own strength but abandons himself to the Lord with total trust.

1. Historical-Religious Overview and Message

In the post-exilic period the term «poor» assumes an increasingly spiritual valence. In the Psalms (22, 25, 34, 37, 69, 86, 109, 149) emerges the figure of the 'anaw (plural: 'anawim): one who is humble before God, who recognizes himself as needing His help, who does not count on his own resources but entrusts himself totally to the Lord.

This spirituality develops especially in the centuries preceding the coming of Christ: the poor become the faithful «remnant» of Israel, the authentic nucleus of the people of God. In this context «poor of God» is a title of honor: it designates one whose heart is open to God, who welcomes His Word, who awaits with patience the salvation of the Lord.

2. Self-Portrait

The «poor of God» portray themselves in the Psalms with precise traits. They are the humble ('anawim), the meek, those who acknowledge their limits as creatures. They have an unshakeable trust in the Lord: «The poor will eat and be satisfied; those who seek him will praise the Lord» (Ps 22:27). They feel themselves to be the «people of God» par excellence: «For the Lord takes delight in his people; he crowns the humble with salvation» (Ps 149:4). Their prayer is made of abandonment, of confident waiting, of grateful praise.

Introduction

The prayer of the «poor of God» is an act that arises from the awareness of one's existential poverty before God and that expresses itself in characteristic forms, recognizable in the Psalter and in sapiential literature.

1. Adoration and Acknowledgment

The first characteristic is adoration and acknowledgment of the sovereignty of God. The «poor of God» knows that God is everything and he is nothing; for this reason his prayer arises from an attitude of profound reverence.

a) Adoration

Adoration is the acknowledgment of the absolute greatness of God as manifested in history. The poor adores God not because he obtains something, but because God is God: «Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised» (Ps 48:2).

b) Acknowledgment

Alongside adoration there is acknowledgment of the benefits received: the poor knows that he has received everything from God and acknowledges it to him with gratitude. «Praise the Lord, my soul, and forget not all his benefits» (Ps 103:2).

2. The Psalms: Prayer of the Poor of God

The Psalter is the book of prayer of the «poor of God». The Psalms express the full range of feelings of the human heart in relation to God: praise, supplication, thanksgiving, lament, trust, repentance. In them the spirituality of the 'anawim is reflected: the trusting abandonment to God in tribulation, the certainty that the Lord hears the cry of the poor, the joy of the saved who praises God.

Introduction

The prayer of the «poor of God» is not immune to obstacles. Indeed, the three central chapters of the book address precisely the temptations that put the life of prayer at risk: the intellectual temptation, the temptation of sensibility, and the temptation of action.

1. The Intellectual Temptation

The first temptation is the intellectual one: wanting to understand everything before praying, demanding that God answer one's questions, subordinating faith to reason. The «poor of God» knows instead that prayer precedes and nourishes understanding; he knows that one enters into the mystery of God not with the mind alone, but with an open and available heart.

2. The Temptation of Sensibility

The second temptation is that of sensibility: identifying the quality of prayer with one's own emotional and affective states, seeking sensible consolations, becoming discouraged when prayer seems arid and without fruit. The «poor of God» knows instead that prayer is made above all of fidelity and will, not of feelings.

3. The Temptation of Action

The third temptation is that of action: believing that doing is more important than praying, privileging efficiency over the contemplative. The «poor of God» knows instead that action is born from prayer and returns to it; he knows that without prayer action loses its foundation and its direction.

Introduction

Jesus is the «poor of God» par excellence. In him is fulfilled and surpassed the entire biblical tradition of the «poor of God» of the Old Testament. His poverty is not only economic, but is that radical spiritual poverty that makes him totally available to the Father and fully in solidarity with humanity.

1. The Messiah Awaited in the Old Testament

The Old Testament foretells the Messiah as the «poor» par excellence. In Zechariah 9:9 the messianic king enters Jerusalem «humble, riding on a donkey»: the Messiah is not a powerful one of the earth, but one who comes in the name of the Lord with the humility and gentleness of the «poor of God». The Servant of the Lord of Isaiah (Is 42–53) realizes this figure: he is the one who does not shout, does not raise his voice in the streets, does not break the bruised reed, does not snuff out the smoldering wick (Is 42:2-3).

2. The Messiah in the New Testament

In the New Testament Jesus reveals himself as the fulfillment of this expectation. The Beatitudes (Mt 5:3-12) are his identity card: «Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven». Jesus defines himself as «meek and humble of heart» (Mt 11:29) and invites his disciples to take his yoke upon themselves. His birth in Bethlehem, his hidden life in Nazareth, his radical poverty in public ministry, his ignominious death on the cross: everything is an expression of his «poverty» as total abandonment to the Father and total gift to humanity.

Introduction

The Gospels offer us a series of precious testimonies on the personal prayer of Jesus. This is not a formal or ritual prayer, but a profound and continuous experience of communion with the Father, which is the center and foundation of all his life and mission.

1. Jesus at Prayer in the Gospels

The Synoptic Gospels, especially Luke, present Jesus in prayer at the crucial moments of his life: at the baptism in the Jordan (Lk 3:21), before the choice of the Twelve (Lk 6:12), at the transfiguration (Lk 9:28-29), in the garden of Gethsemane (Lk 22:41-44), on the cross (Lk 23:34.46). Prayer is not for Jesus a moment among others: it is the breath of his existence, the place where his relationship with the Father is rooted.

2. Prayer as an Interior Attitude

The prayer of Jesus is not only an explicit moment of conversation with the Father, but is also and above all a permanent interior attitude: the awareness of being the beloved Son of the Father, sent into the world for the salvation of humanity. It is this filial awareness that permeates his every act, his every word, his every choice. The prayer of Jesus is therefore the perfect realization of that spiritual poverty of the «poor of God» of the Old Testament: total abandonment to the Father.

Introduction

Alongside the personal prayer of Jesus, the Gospels have preserved for us some of his concrete prayers, which allow us to grasp the characteristic traits of his relationship with the Father.

1. Prayers Linked to His Mission

Some prayers of Jesus are closely linked to his mission. The cry on the cross: «Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing» (Lk 23:34) is the supreme expression of his solidarity with sinful humanity. The high priestly prayer of John 17 is the great prayer of intercession in which Jesus prays for his disciples and for all those who will believe in him.

2. Prayers Linked to His Life

Other prayers accompany significant moments of Jesus' life. The hymn of jubilation (Mt 11:25-26): «I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and have revealed them to infants». The prayer in Gethsemane (Lk 22:42): «Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me; yet, not my will but yours be done». The last word on the cross (Lk 23:46): «Father, into your hands I commend my spirit».

Introduction

Mary represents the summit and fulfillment of the spirituality of the «poor of God» of the Old Testament. In her is concentrated the entire tradition of the 'anawim and the way is opened to the new reality of the New Testament.

Let us recall what was said about the «poor of God» of the Old Testament, especially those of the post-exilic period. In that period the «poor» constitute the qualitative element of Israel and constitute the so-called «remnant», which alone merits in the eyes of the prophets the title of «people of God». In Ps 149 these «poor» feel themselves to be the people of God: «For the Lord takes delight in his people; he crowns the humble with salvation».

Now, Mary represents the best part of this «remnant», its finest expression, its final maturation and fulfillment. Mary is the richest and most beautiful fruit of that multitude of «poor of God» of the post-exilic period. Her voice, which we will hear in the Magnificat, constitutes an admirable synthesis of that chain, that legion of pray-ers. Mary condenses in the Magnificat all the various resonances of the choirs of the Psalter.

1. Mary, the «Poor Woman» of God

The account of the Annunciation in Lk 1:26-38 represents a very dense and complete synthesis of all biblical Mariology. Luke notes the very strong antithesis between the situation of the Baptist and that of Christ: the facts of the Baptist's origin are placed in a climate of apotheosis; those of Christ's origin are found instead in a situation of humility, of shadow, almost of anonymity.

An element by no means indifferent to the meaning of the announcement to Mary: it underlines the nothingness and emptiness of the creature. Nazareth, a little-regarded place; the person of Mary: a girl of the people whose name is barely known; the moment: also diluted in chronological anonymity. All these data, in contrast to those of the Baptist, truly represent the nothingness and emptiness of the creature. Mary, however, constitutes with her nothingness and her emptiness the total availability of the creature before God.

2. The Faith of Mary

It is indicative that the first beatitude of the Gospel of Luke is found on the lips of Elizabeth, when she addresses Mary and says to her: «Blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord» (Lk 1:45). Mary, the «poor of God», precisely for the type of faith she lived, is the ideal poor woman of the Kingdom. Her faith possesses four unmistakable characteristics.

a) The «Fiducial» Faith of Mary

Mary lived above all an intense fiducial faith, which became gift and total abandonment to God. We know of the drama that the Virgin experienced faced with the awareness of her messianic motherhood. When, however, she realized that she was in the line of God's will, she answered without hesitation: «Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word» (Lk 1:38).

b) The «Gift/Abandonment» Faith of Mary

This fiducial faith of Mary flows naturally into faith as gift and abandonment, a typically Lukan theme. Mary copies the example of Jesus, gives herself completely to God in faith as gift, complete abandonment of herself.

c) The «Commitment» Faith of Mary

Mary, however, also gives herself completely to her neighbor. Her faith, which trusts totally in God by giving herself radically to him, becomes a faith of commitment.

d) The «Joyful Stripping» Faith of Mary

The gift of self in the commitment of one's faith does not give Mary the awareness of feeling like a creditor before God. On the contrary, she always feels herself to be a debtor before God. The Magnificat is revealing of this her spiritual climate.

Introduction

The Magnificat is a wonderful song of praise, it is the expression of a soul entirely turned toward God. As regards Our Lady, we are immensely fortunate, because we have an inspired spiritual biography of hers, and this her spiritual biography is given precisely by the Magnificat.

1. Its Literary Context

To grasp all the richness of its doctrinal message one must pay attention to the point in the Gospel where Luke places it. The Magnificat comes immediately after the announcement of the messianic motherhood of Mary and after the episode of the visit to Elizabeth. The Magnificat is therefore a direct response in a particular way to the final beatitude of the account of the Virgin's visit to Elizabeth.

2. Its Structure and Content

Its structure is very simple: it comprises an introduction, followed by two parts. The introduction is given by vv. 46-47: «My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior».

The first part encompasses vv. 48-50: «For he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name».

The second part is constituted by vv. 51-53: «He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts. He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly; he has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty».

The conclusion is given by vv. 54-55: «He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever».

3. The Magnificat in the Life of Mary

One must say first of all that the Magnificat must be seen in the evangelical perspective in which it has been placed. The song says not only what Mary felt and lived in herself at that moment, but also how Mary thought over and understood that event after the resurrection. In this sense the Magnificat is an «authorized document of Mary's paschal meditation».

4. The Prayer Message of the Magnificat

In the first part Mary proclaims what God has done in her and sees this work of the Lord as a great enterprise of God; she feels herself at the center, in the heart of the history of salvation, and grasps herself as an instrument of the most astonishing divine marvels. All this overwhelms her with admiration for the mercy of God in the face of her wretchedness.

In the second part we have Mary's sapiential meditation on the action of God in history. Mary reads her personal experience within the broad picture of human events and grasps and celebrates with gratitude the loving and salvific conduct of God.

Introduction

The Christian is a «poor of God» because he has the spirit of a child in the sense intended by Jesus, and this datum constitutes the specific of his identity. Let us now examine the Gospel message on the identity of the Christian as «poor of God», because a child of the Kingdom.

1. The Identity of the Christian as «Poor of God»

Let us start from the Beatitude of Mt 5:3: «Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven». The term «spirit» in the Bible connotes «strength, energy, power» and is said above all of God, because the Spirit is a good of his exclusive property. The specification «poor in spirit» indicates those who have the spirit of the truly poor, who are poor before God.

Mt 5:3 therefore offers the synthetic and global definition of the Christian, helps us to understand the poverty of which it speaks in a religious sense and not in a vague sense. In this situation the poor person blessed by the Gospel is the poor person who has been helped by his socioeconomic condition to welcome the gratuity of God, to recognize his own dependence on Him.

2. The Origin of This Poverty: The Spirit of a Child (Mt 18:1-4)

The origin of this identity of the Christian resides in the possession of that spirit of a child as presented to us by Mt 18:1-4. Let us note how v. 3 begins: «Truly I tell you, unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever becomes humble like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven». The child is taken here as a point of comparison. The specific proper of the child is given by his inability to provide for himself, by the absence of self-sufficiency; the child is a personified limit and an existential dependence on others.

3. The Existential Radicality of the Poverty of the Disciple

The datum of the objective radicality of the believer is found in Jn 3:3-5. We are in the encounter with Nicodemus, who in Jn 3 appears as the representative of the imperfect believer. Jesus affirms: «Very truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God without being born from above» (v. 3). Here then are the two fundamental conditions for entry into the Kingdom: the baptism of water and the recreative work of the Spirit. Christian life implies a true rebirth: one is born «again». But one is reborn under the impulse of God, with the absolutely necessary intervention of his Spirit.

Introduction

Let us now consider the specific prayer of the Christian: the Our Father. It is the prayer that Jesus taught his disciples and that the entire Christian tradition has always felt as one of the most precious data of the heritage that he has left us.

1. Its Context and Structure

We know that in the Gospels we have two formulations of this prayer: that of Mt 6:9-13 and that offered to us by Lk 11:2-4. The Lukan version: «Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us. And do not bring us to the time of trial». In the structure of the Our Father we have a solemn introductory invocation and then two parts: the first contains three petitions addressed to God; the second contains three requests concerning humanity.

2. Analysis of the Contents

a) «Our Father who art in heaven»

Invoking God in this way is equivalent to recognizing oneself as children of God and, consequently, as brothers and sisters among ourselves. From this formulation emerges the awareness that, as Christians, one never prays alone, but always turns to God in communion with all those who are children of God.

b) First Part: The Three Petitions

«Hallowed be your name»: to hallow the name of God means to recognize that God is totally different from us, that He is the totally Other, that He is the Absolute, the Transcendent, the Infinite. «Your kingdom come»: the Kingdom of God preached by Jesus is that existential situation in which between God and humanity a full communion is realized. «Your will be done»: God does not coerce us, but offers himself, proposes himself. With this petition we ask God to realize his will and that we may know how to respect and welcome his will of salvation.

c) Second Part: The Three Requests

«Give us this day our daily bread»: certainly we ask the Lord for what is necessary for daily life, but in the perspective of the believer the horizons are much broader. «Forgive us our debts as we also have forgiven our debtors»: «debtor» expresses the situation of humanity before God. The human person before God is always the insolvent debtor, above all because he is a sinner. «Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil»: here we are not asking to be protected from normal daily temptations, but to be protected from that trial which is capable of provoking in us apostasy.
